before.content_html:
Why 1912 Matters

J.B. Priestley set An Inspector Calls in 1912 but wrote it in 1945. That thirty-three-year gap is the engine of the entire play. In 1912, the Edwardian elite believed their world was permanent: the British Empire was vast, the class system felt unshakeable, and industrialists like Arthur Birling could dismiss any talk of war or social change. By 1945, two world wars had destroyed millions of lives, the Empire was crumbling, and a Labour government was about to create the Welfare State. Priestley’s audience knew everything that the Birlings did not.

This is why dramatic irony is the play’s most powerful weapon. When Arthur Birling announces that the Titanic is “unsinkable, absolutely unsinkable” and that there will be no war, the 1945 audience would have laughed — and then felt uneasy. Priestley is telling them: if the confident men of 1912 were so catastrophically wrong, what are today’s leaders getting wrong right now?

Key Fact

Birling’s speech in Act 1 contains at least three spectacularly wrong predictions: the Titanic is “unsinkable,” there will be no war (“the Germans don’t want war”), and technology will bring “a time of steadily increasing prosperity.” A 1945 audience had lived through two world wars, the sinking of the Titanic, and the Great Depression — making every word a mark of arrogant foolishness.

Edwardian England: Class and Capitalism

The Edwardian period was an age of extreme inequality. Factory owners like Birling paid low wages to maximise profit, and workers — especially women — had very few rights. Trade unions were growing but could be easily crushed: Birling boasts that he sacked Eva Smith for her part in a strike demanding a modest pay rise from twenty-two shillings and sixpence to twenty-five shillings a week. He describes the strikers as wanting “the earth” and sees no moral problem with firing them. His philosophy is clear: “a man has to mind his own business and look after himself and his own.”

Priestley uses Birling to represent everything he believed was wrong with capitalism. Birling treats people as units of production, not as human beings. His obsession with profit, status, and respectability blinds him to any sense of collective responsibility. This is precisely the attitude Priestley wanted his 1945 audience to reject.

Priestley was a committed socialist who had served in the First World War and witnessed its horrors first-hand. During the Second World War, his BBC radio broadcasts — the Postscripts — reached millions and argued passionately that after the war, Britain must build a fairer society. His broadcasts were so popular (and so politically charged) that Churchill’s government pressured the BBC into cancelling them.

In 1945, Priestley helped found the Common Wealth Party and championed the ideas that led to the Labour landslide election victory and the creation of the NHS, free education, and social security. An Inspector Calls is a dramatic manifesto for this new society: the Inspector’s final speech — “We are members of one body. We are responsible for each other” — is Priestley speaking directly to his audience, urging them to vote for a world where people like Eva Smith are protected, not discarded.

The Time Gap as a Dramatic Device

Setting the play in 1912 allows Priestley to do something brilliantly theatrical. The audience is positioned as judges. They already know the Birlings’ comfortable world will be shattered by the First World War (1914–1918), the General Strike (1926), the Great Depression (1929–1939), and the Second World War (1939–1945). Every confident statement Birling makes about progress and peace is undercut by history. The audience does not need the Inspector to tell them Birling is wrong — they already know.

This time gap also gives the Inspector’s warning its full force. When he speaks of “fire and blood and anguish,” the 1945 audience had literally just lived through that fire and blood. Priestley is saying: these catastrophes happened because people like the Birlings refused to accept responsibility. If you repeat their selfishness, it will happen again.

Key Fact

The thirty-three-year gap between setting (1912) and performance (1945) transforms the entire play into an exercise in dramatic irony. Every Birling assumption about stability, prosperity, and peace is demolished by history — and the audience becomes a moral jury, already knowing the verdict before the Inspector arrives.

Priestley wrote the play at a turning point in British history. The war was ending, and the country faced a choice: return to the old class system, or build something fairer. The 1945 general election offered exactly this choice — Churchill’s Conservatives versus Attlee’s Labour. Priestley wanted his audience to see the Birlings as a warning from the past. If Britain went back to Birling’s selfish individualism, the cycle of suffering would continue. The play premiered in Moscow in 1945 (before London), partly because the Soviet Union’s socialist values aligned with Priestley’s message, and partly because London theatres were fully booked.

The play’s enduring power comes from this dual time frame. It is not just a detective story about one girl’s death — it is a political argument about the kind of society we choose to live in.

“Public Men Have Responsibilities as Well as Privileges”

This line, spoken by the Inspector in Act 1, directly challenges Birling’s philosophy. Birling believes that wealth and status give him the right to act as he pleases. The Inspector insists that power comes with obligation. For the Eduqas exam, this quotation is a key link to AO4 (context): Priestley is drawing on his own experience of how the privileged classes failed ordinary people before both world wars, and arguing that post-war Britain must hold its leaders to account.
before.exam_tip_html: For the Eduqas two-part question, part (a) asks how Priestley presents a theme or character in the printed extract. Part (b) asks how the same theme or character is presented elsewhere in the play. In a context question, do not bolt on a paragraph about “1912 vs 1945” — instead, weave context into your analysis of specific quotations. For example: “Birling’s claim that the Titanic is ‘unsinkable’ would have provoked dark laughter from Priestley’s 1945 audience, who knew the ship sank on its maiden voyage.” This earns AO4 marks through embedded analysis, not bolted-on paragraphs.

before.content_html:
The Engagement Dinner: A World of Privilege

Act 1 opens on a scene of smug celebration. The Birling family are gathered around a dining table to celebrate the engagement of Sheila Birling to Gerald Croft. The stage directions describe “a fairly large suburban house” with “good solid furniture” — comfortable but not fashionable. The lighting should be “pink and intimate” until the Inspector arrives, when it turns “brighter and harder.” This is not a casual detail: Priestley uses the lighting shift to signal that the Birlings’ rosy, self-satisfied world is about to be exposed to harsh scrutiny.

The dinner itself reveals the family’s priorities. Arthur Birling is more excited about the business benefits of the engagement — a potential merger with Gerald’s father’s company, Crofts Limited — than about his daughter’s happiness. He tells Gerald: “Your father and I have been friendly rivals in business … now you’ve brought us together.” The language of commerce (“rivals,” “business”) invades what should be a personal, emotional moment. Priestley immediately signals that for Birling, relationships are transactions.

Key Fact

The lighting shift from “pink and intimate” to “brighter and harder” is one of Priestley’s most important stage directions. It symbolises the movement from the Birlings’ comfortable self-deception to the uncomfortable truths the Inspector will force them to confront. In the exam, this is a strong example of how Priestley uses dramatic techniques (AO2) to convey meaning.

Birling’s Speech: Confidence and Catastrophe

After the women leave the dining room (a standard Edwardian social convention that itself reveals gender inequality), Birling delivers his infamous speech to Gerald and Eric. He dismisses the threat of war — “the Germans don’t want war” — and praises the Titanic as “unsinkable, absolutely unsinkable.” He mocks “cranks” who talk about community and insists that “a man has to mind his own business and look after himself and his own.”

This speech is Priestley’s most concentrated use of dramatic irony. Every prediction is wrong. The Titanic sank on 15 April 1912. The First World War began in 1914. The Great Depression devastated millions. Birling’s confidence is not just misplaced — it is dangerous, because it comes from a man who refuses to look beyond his own interests. Priestley invites the 1945 audience to laugh at Birling, but also to recognise that this kind of arrogant self-assurance led directly to catastrophe.

The Inspector’s arrival is timed with devastating precision. Birling is mid-sentence, lecturing Gerald and Eric about how “a man has to mind his own business,” when the doorbell rings “sharp.” The stage direction “sharp” is crucial — the sound cuts through Birling’s complacency like a blade. Priestley uses this dramatic interruption to undermine everything Birling has just said. The Inspector is the physical embodiment of the community Birling has dismissed. His very existence disproves Birling’s philosophy that a man can live for himself alone.

The timing also foreshadows the play’s structure: every time a character tries to assert their innocence or change the subject, the Inspector steers them back. He controls the pace of revelation, and no one — not even the wealthy Birling — can stop him.

Eva Smith: The Girl Nobody Cared About

The Inspector announces that a girl called Eva Smith has died in the Infirmary after swallowing strong disinfectant. He shows Birling a photograph — but only Birling. This is a deliberate technique: by showing the photograph to one character at a time, the Inspector (and Priestley) controls who speaks and prevents the family from collaborating on a story. It also raises the question that will haunt the play’s ending: is it even the same girl?

Birling recognises Eva as a former employee. She was a good worker — “a lively good-looking girl” — but she helped organise a strike for higher wages. Birling sacked her. He is entirely unapologetic: “If you don’t come down sharply on some of these people, they’d soon be asking for the earth.” Notice the dehumanising language: “these people” reduces Eva and her fellow workers to a faceless category. Sheila’s challenge is direct and devastating: “these girls aren’t cheap labour — they’re people.”

Key Fact

The Inspector’s line “these girls aren’t cheap labour — they’re people” is the play’s moral core stated early. It directly contradicts Birling’s view of workers as economic units and establishes the Inspector as a voice for collective responsibility. In the Eduqas exam, this quotation connects AO1 (understanding), AO2 (language analysis), and AO4 (Priestley’s socialist context).

Sheila’s Confession at Milwards

After Eva was sacked by Birling, she found work at Milwards, a dress shop. Sheila Birling had her fired out of jealousy. She admits she was in a bad temper, tried on a dress that didn’t suit her, and caught Eva holding the dress against herself and smiling. Sheila saw that the dress “just suited her” and was “furious.” She threatened the shop manager that if Eva was not dismissed, the Birlings would close their account. Eva lost her job.

Sheila’s reaction to her own confession is crucial — it distinguishes her from her parents. She is “miserably” ashamed: “I know I’m to blame — and I’m desperately sorry.” Unlike Birling, who sees nothing wrong with his actions, Sheila immediately accepts responsibility. This is the beginning of her moral transformation, and Priestley uses her to represent the younger generation’s capacity for change. Her character arc from spoilt, thoughtless girl to morally aware young woman is one of the play’s most important developments.

Sheila’s ability to have Eva sacked reveals the hidden violence of the class system. She did not physically harm Eva; she simply exercised the power that comes with wealth and social status. The Milwards manager could not refuse a wealthy customer’s demand. Eva, as a working-class woman with no protection, was entirely vulnerable. Priestley shows that class power does not need to be dramatic or visible to be destructive — a casual threat from a privileged customer can ruin a life.

The fact that Sheila was motivated by vanity — not malice — makes it worse in some ways. She did not set out to destroy Eva; she simply never considered that her actions would have consequences for someone beneath her social station. This is precisely the kind of thoughtlessness Priestley wants his audience to examine in themselves.
before.exam_tip_html: In the Eduqas part (a) response, always start by identifying the writer’s technique before analysing its effect. For example, don’t just say “the lighting changes” — say “Priestley uses the stage direction of a lighting shift from ‘pink and intimate’ to ‘brighter and harder’ to symbolise the exposure of the Birlings’ comfortable illusions.” Naming the technique (stage direction, dramatic irony, symbolism) signals AO2 awareness to the examiner.

before.content_html:
Gerald Croft and Daisy Renton

Act 2 begins with the Inspector turning his attention to Gerald Croft. Gerald met Eva Smith — now using the name Daisy Renton — at the Palace Bar, a venue associated with prostitution. He describes her as “very pretty” and “young and fresh and charming.” Gerald rescued her from Alderman Meggarty, a local politician who was harassing her, and set her up in a friend’s flat as his mistress.

Gerald insists the relationship was genuine: “I didn’t feel about her as she felt about me.” But his language reveals uncomfortable truths. He calls her a “pretty girl” repeatedly, and his actions — providing a flat, money, and companionship only when convenient — follow the pattern of a wealthy man keeping a working-class woman as a convenient possession. When he ended the affair, Eva/Daisy “was very gallant — about it” and “didn’t blame” him. Priestley shows that even when upper-class men appear kind, the class power imbalance makes genuine equality impossible.

Key Fact

Gerald’s relationship with Daisy Renton exposes the class power imbalance at the heart of Edwardian gender relations. He provided her with a flat, money, and affection — but always on his terms. When he was done, he walked away unscathed while Eva was left with nothing. Priestley uses Gerald to show that even apparent kindness can be a form of exploitation when one person holds all the power.

The Palace Bar and Alderman Meggarty

The Palace Bar is a significant setting. It was a place where wealthy men met young working-class women, often for sexual exploitation. Gerald admits he “went in there — one night — after a rather long, dull day” and saw Meggarty “wedging” Daisy into a corner. Gerald’s rescue seems noble on the surface, but Priestley complicates it: Gerald replaces one form of male exploitation with another. Meggarty harasses; Gerald possesses. Both men treat Daisy as an object to be used by men of higher status.

Alderman Meggarty is a councillor — a public figure who is supposed to serve the community. His behaviour at the Palace Bar reveals the hypocrisy of the Edwardian establishment: men who present themselves as respectable pillars of society are privately predatory. This connects to the Inspector’s warning that “Public men have responsibilities as well as privileges.”

Gerald occupies a middle ground between the older and younger Birlings. Unlike Arthur and Sybil, he is genuinely moved by Eva’s death and shows some emotional response: “She was pretty and warm-hearted — and intensely grateful.” But unlike Sheila and Eric, he quickly recovers. By Act 3, it is Gerald who investigates whether the Inspector was real and leads the effort to prove the evening was a hoax. He asks: “How do we know she was really Eva Smith or Daisy Renton?”

This makes Gerald a troubling character. His moment of genuine feeling is overwhelmed by his desire to restore the status quo. Priestley uses him to suggest that sympathy without lasting change is not enough. Gerald is sorry, but he will not alter his behaviour or challenge the system that allowed the exploitation. He represents the audience member who feels bad but does nothing.

Mrs Birling’s Refusal: The Charity Committee

The most devastating section of Act 2 belongs to Mrs Birling (Sybil). Eva, now desperate and pregnant, applied to the Brumley Women’s Charity Organisation for help. Mrs Birling, as chair of the committee, used her influence to have Eva’s case rejected. Her reasons reveal breathtaking class prejudice: Eva had used the name “Mrs Birling,” which Sybil found impertinent; Eva’s manner seemed “gross” and she was not sufficiently grateful; and Eva refused to take money from the baby’s father because it was stolen — a scruple that Mrs Birling interprets as evidence of dishonesty rather than integrity.

Mrs Birling insists that the real responsibility lies with “the father of the child” and that he should be made an example of, publicly shamed, and “dealt with very severely.” This is one of Priestley’s most powerful uses of dramatic irony. The audience — and Sheila, who has already guessed — realise that the father is Eric Birling. Mrs Birling is unknowingly demanding that her own son be publicly humiliated.

Key Fact

Mrs Birling’s insistence that the father should “be made an example of” and “confess in public” is the play’s most explosive dramatic irony. She does not know that the father is her own son Eric. Sheila’s frantic attempts to stop her mother — “Mother — stop — stop!” — heighten the tension. Priestley traps Mrs Birling with her own words: she has just argued for the harshest possible punishment of her own child.

Sheila’s Growing Awareness

Throughout Act 2, Sheila becomes increasingly perceptive. She warns Gerald: “You fool — he knows. Of course he knows.” She recognises before anyone else that the Inspector cannot be deflected or deceived. When her mother begins to condemn the father of Eva’s child, Sheila tries desperately to stop her: “Mother — I begged you and begged you to stop.” Sheila’s intelligence and moral awareness separate her from the older generation.

Her engagement ring is a powerful symbol in Act 2. Sheila hands it back to Gerald after learning about Daisy Renton. This is not just a personal decision — it represents Sheila’s rejection of the comfortable, unquestioning life she was expected to lead. The ring symbolised the Birling-Croft business alliance as much as love; by returning it, Sheila steps outside the transactional world her father built. Priestley uses her to model the response he wants from his audience: face uncomfortable truths, accept responsibility, and change.

Mrs Birling’s language is formal, controlled, and dismissive. She refers to Eva as “girls of that class.” She describes Eva’s appeal as giving “a lot of silly, nonsensical things” and says she was “not satisfied” with Eva’s story. The coldness is deliberate: Mrs Birling speaks in the language of institutional authority, not human compassion. She uses her position on the charity to gatekeep who deserves help, applying moral judgements that protect the upper class and punish the vulnerable.

Unlike Birling, whose bluster occasionally reveals anxiety, Mrs Birling never wavers. She is the play’s most unchanging character. Even after the Inspector’s speech, she remains “rather agitated but quite determined.” Priestley presents her as the ultimate failure of the upper class: someone who cannot even imagine that a working-class woman deserves sympathy. She is the static character against whom Sheila and Eric’s growth is measured.
before.exam_tip_html: For Eduqas part (b), you must range across the whole play, not just one scene. A strong answer about Mrs Birling would cover: her refusal at the charity (Act 2), her unchanged attitude in Act 3, and the contrast with Sheila’s growth. Use topic sentences to signal each new point: “Elsewhere in the play, Priestley develops Mrs Birling’s refusal to accept responsibility when…” This structure ensures you cover the ‘elsewhere’ requirement clearly.

before.exam_tip_html: The cyclical ending is a gift for the Eduqas exam. If the extract is from Act 3, you can analyse the phone call as Priestley’s structural masterstroke. For part (b), link the ending to the Inspector’s warning (‘fire and blood and anguish’) and to the 1912/1945 time gap. The cyclical structure proves the Inspector’s point: those who refuse to learn will be forced to repeat the lesson. Always connect structure (AO2) to Priestley’s purpose (AO4).
before.content_html:
Eric’s Confession: Drinking, Theft, and Shame

Act 3 opens with Eric returning to face the Inspector. His involvement with Eva Smith is the most disturbing of all. He met her at the Palace Bar — the same venue where Gerald found her — and forced himself on her while drunk. He admits: “I was in that state when a chap easily turns nasty.” Eva became pregnant, and Eric stole money from his father’s business to support her. He gave her about fifty pounds in total — a substantial sum in 1912 — but Eva refused to accept more because she suspected it was stolen.

Eric’s language throughout his confession reveals both guilt and helplessness. He describes himself not as a villain but as someone who was never given the tools to behave differently. His most revealing line comes when he rounds on his father: “You’re not the kind of father a chap could go to when he’s in trouble.” This accusation is devastating because it redirects blame from Eric’s individual failings to the Birling family’s emotional dysfunction. Birling’s obsession with business, reputation, and status has left his son unable to seek help from his own father. Priestley suggests that dysfunctional family relationships are a product of the capitalist, class-obsessed world the Birlings inhabit.

Key Fact

Eric’s accusation — “You’re not the kind of father a chap could go to when he’s in trouble” — is one of the play’s most important lines. It reveals that Birling’s prioritisation of business and reputation over family has created a household where a son cannot even ask his father for help. Priestley uses this to show that capitalist values corrupt not just society, but personal relationships within the family.

The Inspector’s Final Speech

With all five characters exposed, the Inspector delivers his final speech. It is the play’s climax — a dramatic monologue that functions as Priestley’s direct address to his 1945 audience. The Inspector says:

“But just remember this. One Eva Smith has gone — but there are millions and millions and millions of Eva Smiths and John Smiths still left with us, with their lives, their hopes and fears, their suffering, and chance of happiness, all intertwined with our lives, with what we think and say and do. We don’t live alone. We are members of one body. We are responsible for each other. And I tell you that the time will soon come when, if men will not learn that lesson, then they will be taught it in fire and blood and anguish.”

The speech operates on multiple levels. The repetition of “millions and millions and millions” hammers home the scale of social injustice — Eva is not unique; she represents an entire class of exploited people. “We are members of one body” echoes the Christian principle of the body of Christ (1 Corinthians 12:27), giving the speech a quasi-religious authority. And the warning of “fire and blood and anguish” is both a biblical echo and a direct reference to the two world wars that the 1945 audience had just survived.

The tricolon “fire and blood and anguish” uses the conjunction “and” between each noun (polysyndeton), which slows the rhythm and gives each word equal weight. “Fire” evokes the Blitz; “blood” evokes the trenches and battlefields; “anguish” captures the emotional devastation that lingers after physical destruction. The warning is conditional: “if men will not learn that lesson” — Priestley leaves the door open. The catastrophe is not inevitable; it is a consequence of choosing selfishness over responsibility. The 1945 audience is being told: you have a second chance. Do not waste it.

The biblical register of the speech — “members of one body,” “taught it in fire” — gives the Inspector an almost prophetic authority. He speaks not as a police inspector but as a moral or spiritual force. This links to the mystery of his identity: he may be a ghost, an angel, a time traveller, or simply a dramatic device. What matters is that his message carries the weight of absolute truth.

The Aftermath: Was It a Hoax?

After the Inspector leaves, the Birlings and Gerald react in sharply divided ways. Birling and Mrs Birling immediately try to minimise the evening’s events. Gerald rings the Infirmary and discovers that no girl has died from swallowing disinfectant. Birling is triumphant: “the whole story’s just a lot of moonshine.” He and Gerald piece together the possibility that the Inspector was not a real police officer, and that the photographs shown to each person may have been of different girls. The older generation’s relief is palpable — and, for the audience, deeply unsettling.

Sheila and Eric refuse to join this celebration. Sheila’s response is the play’s moral compass: “You’re pretending everything’s just as it was before.” Eric agrees: “I don’t see much nonsense about it when a girl goes and kills herself. You lot may be letting yourselves out nicely, but I can’t.” The generational divide is absolute. The older characters care about whether they will face consequences; the younger characters care about whether they did wrong.

Key Fact

The split between the generations is Priestley’s clearest structural message. Birling and Mrs Birling are relieved because the Inspector may have been a hoax — their concern is escaping scandal, not moral accountability. Sheila and Eric insist that whether the Inspector was real is irrelevant: they still behaved terribly. Priestley tells his audience that moral responsibility does not depend on whether you get caught.

The Cyclical Ending

The play’s final moments are its most theatrical. Just as the Birlings are congratulating themselves, the telephone rings. Birling answers and reports, ashen-faced: “That was the police. A girl has just died — on her way to the Infirmary — after swallowing some disinfectant. And a police inspector is on his way here — to ask some — questions.”

This cyclical ending is devastating. The entire evening is about to happen again. For the audience, the message is inescapable: if you refuse to learn from the Inspector’s visit, history will repeat itself. The Birlings had a chance to change and rejected it; now they face the consequences. Priestley warns his 1945 audience: you too have been given a chance by the end of the war. Do not be like the Birlings.

The cyclical ending has been interpreted in several ways. One reading is that the Inspector was a supernatural warning — a ghost or time traveller who showed the Birlings what was about to happen, giving them a chance to change. They failed, so the real events now begin. Another reading is that the evening was a moral rehearsal: the Inspector tested their consciences, and the phone call is the real test. A third interpretation is political: Priestley is saying that the 1912 warnings about class, exploitation, and war were ignored, leading to catastrophe. Britain now stands at a similar crossroads in 1945.

What all interpretations share is the idea that ignoring moral responsibility has consequences. The phone call is not just a plot twist — it is Priestley’s final, urgent warning. The audience leaves the theatre knowing that the cycle will continue unless people change.

before.content_html:
Arthur Birling: Capitalism Personified

Arthur Birling is a wealthy factory owner, a magistrate, and a former Lord Mayor of Brumley. He is described in the stage directions as “a heavy-looking, rather portentous man” — the adjective “portentous” suggests someone who takes himself very seriously, but the word also means “ominous,” hinting that Birling’s arrogance will bring consequences. He is a social climber: his wife is “his social superior” and he is desperate for a knighthood. Every decision he makes is driven by profit, reputation, or both.

Birling’s defining quotation is “a man has to mind his own business and look after himself and his own.” This is not just a personal philosophy — it is the capitalist creed that Priestley wants to dismantle. Birling sacks Eva for striking, cares more about his knighthood than her death, and celebrates when the Inspector appears to be a hoax. He is the play’s representative figure for selfish capitalism, and Priestley makes him unchanging to show that this ideology is beyond redemption.

Key Fact

Birling is driven by profit, reputation, and status. He sacks Eva to protect profits, fears the Inspector because of his knighthood, and is relieved when the evening seems to be a hoax because it means no scandal. Priestley uses him as a warning: this is what happens when a society prioritises wealth over people.

Sybil Birling: The Ice of the Upper Class

Mrs Birling is described as “a rather cold woman” and “her husband’s social superior.” Where Arthur is loud and blustering, Sybil is controlled and icy. Her class prejudice is absolute: she refers to Eva as “girls of that class” and finds her use of the name “Mrs Birling” “impertinent.” She is the chair of the Brumley Women’s Charity Organisation, which makes her rejection of Eva even more damning — the person whose job it is to help the vulnerable is the one who turns Eva away.

Mrs Birling is the play’s most static character. She never accepts responsibility. Even after the Inspector’s speech, she remains “rather agitated but quite determined.” Priestley uses her to show that the upper class is not just selfish but structurally incapable of empathy. Her inability to recognise Eva as a human being — rather than as a member of a lower class — is the coldest cruelty in the play.

Sheila begins the play as a spoilt, materialistic young woman — “Oh — it’s wonderful!” she exclaims about her engagement ring, with a revealing exclamation that shows how sheltered and superficial her life has been. Her confession at Milwards reveals how casually she wielded her class power to have Eva sacked. But unlike her parents, Sheila is immediately and genuinely ashamed: “I know I’m to blame — and I’m desperately sorry.”

By Act 2, Sheila has become the Inspector’s ally. She warns Gerald: “You fool — he knows.” She returns her engagement ring, rejecting the comfortable life her parents planned for her. By Act 3, she directly confronts her parents: “You’re pretending everything’s just as it was before.” Priestley uses Sheila’s transformation to show that the younger generation can learn, can change, and can reject the values of their parents. She is the audience’s model: recognise your complicity, feel genuine remorse, and act differently.

Eric Birling: Weakness Turned to Moral Strength

Eric is introduced as “not quite at ease, half shy, half assertive” — a young man who does not fit comfortably into his family’s world. He drinks heavily (his mother is the last to know), and his treatment of Eva is the most violent: he forces himself on her while drunk and then steals money from his father’s business to support her. His behaviour is inexcusable, but Priestley complicates our judgement by showing that Eric is also a product of his environment.

Eric’s most powerful moment is his accusation: “You’re not the kind of father a chap could go to when he’s in trouble.” This line exposes the emotional emptiness of the Birling household. Eric’s weakness is partly caused by a family that values respectability over honesty. By the end of the play, Eric has grown. He refuses to celebrate when the Inspector is discredited: “You lot may be letting yourselves out nicely, but I can’t.” Like Sheila, he accepts responsibility regardless of consequences.

Key Fact

Sheila and Eric are the play’s dynamic characters. Both begin as products of privilege, both do terrible things to Eva, and both are transformed by the Inspector’s visit. Priestley uses their change to argue that the younger generation can build a better society — if they choose to learn from the past.

Gerald Croft: The Comfortable Compromise

Gerald is the son of Sir George Croft, which makes him socially superior to the Birlings. He is charming, confident, and emotionally affected by Daisy Renton’s death. But his sympathy is temporary. By Act 3, he is leading the investigation to prove the Inspector was a fraud: “How do we know she was really Eva Smith or Daisy Renton?” Gerald represents the person who feels genuine emotion but ultimately retreats to the safety of the status quo. Priestley suggests that feeling sorry is not enough — what matters is whether you change your behaviour.

The Inspector is described as creating “an impression of massiveness, solidity, and purposefulness.” He is not physically large, but his moral authority fills the room. He controls the pace of the evening, showing each character the photograph one at a time, and he cannot be interrupted, deflected, or bullied. His name — Goole — is a homophone of “ghoul,” suggesting something supernatural or death-related.

The Inspector functions on multiple levels: as a detective figure who uncovers the truth; as a moral judge who forces each character to confront their guilt; as a mouthpiece for Priestley’s socialist beliefs; and as a supernatural or symbolic presence whose true nature is never explained. His final speech — “We are members of one body. We are responsible for each other” — is the play’s thesis statement. Whether he is a ghost, an angel, or a dramatic device, his message is Priestley’s: collective responsibility is not optional.
before.exam_tip_html: In the Eduqas exam, character questions often ask how Priestley ‘presents’ a character. This means you must analyse the writer’s methods (AO2) — not just describe what the character does. For example, do not just say “Birling is selfish.” Say: “Priestley presents Birling as selfish through his monosyllabic, assertive declaration that ‘a man has to mind his own business,’ which is positioned immediately before the Inspector’s arrival to dramatise its failure.” Method + evidence + effect = high marks.

before.content_html:
The Three Unities

Priestley structures An Inspector Calls around the three unities of classical drama: unity of time, unity of place, and unity of action. The entire play takes place in the Birlings’ dining room on a single evening, and the plot follows one continuous investigation. This tight structure is not accidental — it creates a pressure-cooker effect. The characters cannot escape. They cannot go home, sleep on it, or consult lawyers. They are trapped in the room with the Inspector and with each other, and every revelation makes the tension worse.

The unity of place is especially significant. The Birlings’ dining room is their territory — a space of wealth, comfort, and control. The Inspector invades this space and systematically dismantles its security. By the end of the play, the room that symbolised privilege and safety has become a courtroom where the family is judged. Priestley turns the Birlings’ own home against them.

Key Fact

By observing the three unities (one place, one evening, one plot), Priestley creates a claustrophobic structure that mirrors the Inspector’s moral pressure. The characters cannot escape the investigation, just as the audience cannot escape Priestley’s argument. This structural discipline is a deliberate dramatic choice that makes the play feel relentless.

Real-Time Action and Pacing

The play runs in approximately real time — the events on stage take roughly as long as the audience’s experience of watching them. This creates a powerful sense of immediacy. There are no flashbacks, no time jumps, and no relief. Each character is exposed in turn, and the audience watches the family unravel minute by minute. The Inspector controls the pace: he insists on dealing with “one line of enquiry at a time” and refuses to let the Birlings distract him.

Priestley uses the act breaks strategically. Act 1 ends with the Inspector beginning to question Gerald — a cliffhanger that keeps the audience engaged. Act 2 ends with Eric’s entrance after Mrs Birling has unknowingly condemned him. Each break raises the stakes, ensuring the audience returns more invested than before.

The stage directions specify that the lighting should be “pink and intimate” at the start, then become “brighter and harder” when the Inspector arrives. This is Priestley’s most important piece of stage symbolism. The “pink” light represents the Birlings’ rose-tinted view of themselves and their world — warm, comfortable, and flattering. The “brighter and harder” light represents the truth that the Inspector brings: unflattering, inescapable, and exposing.

In a theatre, this shift is visible to the audience and signals the play’s tonal change before a single word is spoken. Priestley understood that drama is not just dialogue — the physical production carries meaning. In the Eduqas exam, analysing this lighting shift demonstrates strong AO2 awareness (writer’s methods).

The Doorbell as Structural Device

The doorbell rings at exactly the moment Birling is lecturing Gerald and Eric about self-reliance: “a man has to mind his own business and look after himself.” The stage direction “sharp” indicates the sound is sudden, cutting, and authoritative. Priestley uses this structural timing to dramatise the failure of Birling’s philosophy. The Inspector — representing community, responsibility, and the outside world — literally interrupts Birling’s speech about individualism. The message is clear: you cannot shut out society, no matter how thick your walls or how loud your speeches.

Dramatic Irony Throughout the Play

Dramatic irony is not limited to Birling’s speech. It operates throughout the play at multiple levels. Mrs Birling’s demand that the father of Eva’s child be “made an example of” is dramatically ironic because the father is her own son. Gerald’s investigation to discredit the Inspector is ironic because the phone call at the end proves the events are real. Even the play’s title contains irony: the Inspector “calls” in both senses — he visits the house, and he calls out their behaviour.

The broadest dramatic irony, however, is the time gap. The 1945 audience knows that the Birlings’ comfortable 1912 world will be destroyed by two world wars. Every expression of confidence, every dismissal of social change, every assertion that all is well — all of it is undercut by the audience’s knowledge of what comes next. Priestley positions his audience as the ultimate judges of the Birling family.

Key Fact

Dramatic irony operates at every level of the play: Birling’s false predictions (1912 vs 1945 knowledge), Mrs Birling’s unwitting condemnation of Eric, the title’s double meaning (“calls” = visits AND calls out), and the audience’s role as moral judges who know the future the characters cannot see. For the exam, identifying multiple layers of irony shows sophisticated analysis.

The Cyclical Structure

The play’s ending is its most powerful structural device. Just as the Birlings have convinced themselves the evening was a hoax, the telephone rings: a real girl has died, and a real inspector is on his way. This cyclical structure means the play could begin again from the start. The Birlings are trapped in a loop of their own making — because they refused to learn the first time, they must face the lesson again.

This is Priestley’s most urgent message to his 1945 audience. The two world wars were the “fire and blood and anguish” that resulted from ignoring the lessons of social responsibility. If Britain returns to the selfish individualism of the Birlings, the cycle will repeat. The cyclical ending transforms the play from a detective story into a political warning.

Structure is assessed through AO2. When writing about structure, always link the technique to its effect on the audience. Do not just name it — explain why Priestley chose it. For example: “Priestley uses a cyclical structure to suggest that the Birlings’ refusal to accept responsibility will trap them in an endless loop of consequences. The final phone call mirrors the Inspector’s arrival in Act 1, creating a sense of inescapability that reinforces the play’s message: moral responsibility cannot be avoided, only delayed.”

Strong structural points for the Eduqas exam include: the three unities (claustrophobic pressure), the lighting shift (exposure of truth), the doorbell (interruption of selfish philosophy), the act-ending cliffhangers (escalating tension), and the cyclical ending (the consequences of inaction).

For part (b), the cyclical ending is a versatile point — you can link it to almost any theme (responsibility, class, generational divide) because the structure itself carries Priestley’s message.

before.content_html:
Who — or What — Is Inspector Goole?

The Inspector’s identity is the play’s central mystery. Gerald discovers that “there is no Inspector Goole” on the local police force. The family rings the Infirmary and learns that no girl has died. For a few moments, it seems the entire evening was a fabrication. But then the telephone rings, and a real girl has died, and a real inspector is coming. So who was Goole? Priestley deliberately refuses to answer. The ambiguity is the point: what matters is not who the Inspector is, but what he represents.

His name is a crucial clue. “Goole” is a homophone of “ghoul” — a spirit associated with death and the grave. This links the Inspector to the supernatural and to Eva’s death. It also echoes the idea that the Inspector is a figure from beyond the natural world, sent to deliver a moral warning. Other interpretations include: a time traveller who knows the future (he predicts the phone call), an angel or divine messenger (his speech has biblical authority), or a manifestation of the Birlings’ collective guilt.

Key Fact

The Inspector has been interpreted as: (1) a ghost or ghoul (his name, his knowledge of Eva’s death), (2) a time traveller (he predicts the phone call), (3) a divine/moral agent (his speech echoes 1 Corinthians 12:27), (4) a dramatic device (he exists to deliver Priestley’s message). In the exam, the strongest approach is to acknowledge the ambiguity and argue that Priestley keeps his identity open precisely because it does not matter — the message matters.

The Inspector as Socialist Mouthpiece

The Inspector’s views align exactly with Priestley’s. His assertion that “Public men have responsibilities as well as privileges” directly challenges Birling’s capitalist creed. His rebuke to Birling — “these girls aren’t cheap labour — they’re people” — is a socialist statement about the dignity of labour. And his final speech — “We are members of one body. We are responsible for each other” — is Priestley’s manifesto for the post-war Welfare State.

Priestley used the Inspector in the same way he used his BBC Postscripts broadcasts: to speak directly to the British public about social justice. The Inspector’s authority comes not from his police credentials (which turn out to be false) but from the moral force of his argument. He is a dramatic mouthpiece — Priestley’s voice on stage — and his words carry the weight of the playwright’s own experience of war, class inequality, and social injustice.

The phrase “We are members of one body” echoes 1 Corinthians 12:27: “Now you are the body of Christ, and each one of you is a part of it.” This biblical allusion gives the Inspector’s speech a prophetic, almost religious authority. It suggests that social responsibility is not just a political idea but a spiritual duty. For a 1945 audience — many of whom were churchgoers — this language would have resonated deeply.

The choice of “body” is also significant. A body is an interconnected system: if one part suffers, all parts suffer. This is Priestley’s argument against Birling’s individualism. You cannot amputate the working class from society and expect the body to function. The metaphor makes the abstract concept of social responsibility concrete and physical.

The Inspector as Moral Force

The Inspector is described in the stage directions as creating “an impression of massiveness, solidity, and purposefulness.” This description is not physical — it is moral. He is not a large man, but his presence fills the room. He speaks “carefully, weightily,” and he cannot be deflected, charmed, or bullied. When Birling tries to intimidate him by mentioning his friendship with the Chief Constable, the Inspector is unmoved. When Mrs Birling tries to dismiss him with upper-class condescension, he persists. His authority does not come from his rank — it comes from the truth he represents.

Priestley makes the Inspector the only character who sees Eva Smith as a complete human being. While each Birling reduces Eva to a function — worker, shop assistant, mistress, charity case — the Inspector insists on her full humanity. He speaks of “her feelings and her hopes,” her “suffering and chance of happiness.” He is the play’s everyman figure — the conscience that every society needs but that the privileged try to ignore.

Key Fact

The Inspector’s authority is moral, not institutional. He speaks “carefully, weightily” and creates “massiveness, solidity, and purposefulness.” His power comes from truth, not from police credentials (which are false). Priestley shows that moral authority outweighs social status — the Inspector, regardless of who he is, is the most powerful person in the room because he is right.

The Inspector’s Methods: Control and Revelation

The Inspector controls the investigation with precision. He shows the photograph to only one character at a time, preventing them from comparing notes and constructing a joint defence. He insists on dealing with “one line of enquiry at a time,” which forces each character to face their guilt individually before the group dynamic can dilute it. This method is also a structural device: it allows Priestley to build the revelation gradually, with each confession raising the stakes.

His questioning technique is direct and uncompromising. He does not use the polite, deferential language the Birlings expect from a social inferior. When Birling tries to deflect (“I was quite justified — I don’t see that it’s any concern of yours”), the Inspector cuts through: “It might be, you know.” This calm, understated authority is more powerful than any shouting. Priestley gives the Inspector a controlled register that contrasts with Birling’s bluster and Mrs Birling’s condescension.

Every Birling reduces Eva to one dimension: Birling sees a troublesome worker, Sheila sees a rival, Gerald sees a pretty mistress, Mrs Birling sees a dishonest applicant, Eric sees a girl he used. Only the Inspector sees Eva as a whole person with “her feelings and her hopes.” His final speech insists on the millions of “Eva Smiths and John Smiths” whose lives are “intertwined with our lives.”

This is the play’s deepest moral point. The Birlings’ failure is not just that they exploited Eva — it is that they never saw her as fully human. Each person treated her as an object: labour, customer, possession, nuisance, problem. The Inspector demands that the audience see her — and everyone like her — as complete human beings with the same right to dignity, safety, and happiness as the Birlings themselves.

For part (b), connect his role across the play: investigator, moral judge, Priestley’s mouthpiece, everyman figure. Always link to AO4: the Inspector voices Priestley’s socialist beliefs formed by his experience of two world wars.

before.description: Responsibility, class, generational divide, gender, morality, plus Eduqas two-part essay structure.
before.content_html:
Theme: Responsibility

Responsibility is the play’s dominant theme. Every character is shown to have contributed to Eva Smith’s death, and the Inspector’s purpose is to make each one accept their share. Birling sacked her; Sheila had her fired; Gerald used and abandoned her; Mrs Birling rejected her plea for help; Eric assaulted her and stole to support her. No single action killed Eva — it was the cumulative weight of an entire society’s indifference.

Priestley draws a clear distinction between two kinds of responsibility. The first is personal: each Birling must accept what they individually did wrong. The second is collective: the Inspector’s line “We are members of one body. We are responsible for each other” demands that society as a whole takes care of its most vulnerable members. Birling’s philosophy — “a man has to mind his own business” — represents the rejection of collective responsibility. The play’s entire structure exists to demolish that philosophy.

Key Fact

Personal responsibility: each character’s individual actions toward Eva (“I know I’m to blame” — Sheila). Collective responsibility: society’s duty to protect the vulnerable (“We are members of one body. We are responsible for each other” — Inspector). Priestley argues that both are essential: you cannot have a just society without individuals who accept their own guilt AND a system that protects people like Eva.

Theme: Class

Class is the mechanism through which responsibility is avoided. The Birlings feel entitled to treat Eva badly because she is working class. Birling sees her as “cheap labour.” Mrs Birling refers to “girls of that class” as if they are a different species. Gerald’s relationship with Daisy Renton is only possible because the class system gives him power over her. Even Sheila’s act at Milwards depends on the shop manager’s deference to a wealthy customer.

Priestley shows that the class system is not just unfair — it is actively destructive. It allows the powerful to exploit the powerless with impunity, and it prevents empathy by creating a psychological distance between “us” and “them.” Mrs Birling cannot help Eva because she literally cannot see her as a fellow human being. The class lens distorts everything. The Inspector’s role is to strip away that lens and force the Birlings to see Eva as she really was: “not cheap labour” but a person.

The generational divide is Priestley’s structural expression of hope. The older generation — Arthur and Sybil — cannot change. They are too deeply embedded in the class system, too invested in their status, and too emotionally closed to feel genuine remorse. When the Inspector is discredited, they immediately celebrate. Sybil remains “quite determined.” Birling calls the evening “moonshine.”

The younger generation — Sheila and Eric — can change, and do. Sheila says: “You’re pretending everything’s just as it was before.” Eric insists: “You lot may be letting yourselves out nicely, but I can’t.” They accept moral responsibility regardless of consequences. Priestley writes this divide as a message to his 1945 audience: the old world (represented by the older Birlings) failed. The new world must be built by a generation willing to accept responsibility. The 1945 election, in which Labour defeated Churchill, was precisely this moment of generational change.

Theme: Gender and Exploitation

Eva Smith’s journey through the play maps the limited options available to working-class women in 1912. She is a factory worker, a shop assistant, a kept woman, a charity applicant, and finally a suicide. At every stage, men control her fate: Birling fires her, Gerald possesses her, Eric assaults her. Even Mrs Birling, who should understand gender vulnerability, uses her institutional power to reject Eva. Priestley shows that gender and class exploitation are intertwined: Eva is vulnerable not just because she is working class, but because she is a working-class woman in a world run by men of higher status.

The play also critiques the double standards applied to men and women. Gerald’s affair is treated as unfortunate but understandable; Eva is the one who suffers. Eric’s drinking and violence are seen as youthful indiscretions; Eva bears the consequences alone. Priestley exposes a society in which men are forgiven and women are destroyed.

Key Fact

Eva’s journey — factory worker, shop assistant, mistress, charity applicant, suicide — maps the narrow and dangerous paths available to working-class women in Edwardian Britain. At every stage, her fate is controlled by someone with more power: employer, customer, lover, committee chair. Priestley uses her story to argue that gender and class exploitation are structural problems, not individual failings.

Theme: Morality and Conscience

The play asks a simple but profound question: does it matter whether you get caught? After Gerald proves the Inspector may have been a fraud, the family splits. Birling and Mrs Birling believe that if there are no legal consequences, they have done nothing wrong. Sheila and Eric believe that the moral reality — what they did to Eva — exists regardless of whether a real inspector punishes them. Priestley sides firmly with the young: moral conscience should be your guide, not fear of punishment.

This is the play’s ultimate message to its audience. You do not need an Inspector to tell you what is right. You should not wait until a girl dies to examine your own behaviour. The responsibility is yours — every day, in every interaction with the people whose lives are “intertwined with” your own.

For modern drama essays on An Inspector Calls, you will typically be tested on two linked tasks. One focuses closely on a printed extract, asking how Priestley presents a theme or character in that passage. The other asks how the same theme or character is presented elsewhere in the play. Both tasks test AO1 (understanding and response), AO2 (analysis of language, form, and structure), and AO4 (context). Check your exam board's specimen paper for the exact question format and mark allocation.

For close extract work, stay close to the passage. Analyse specific words, phrases, and techniques. Use short embedded quotations. Identify the method before analysing its effect: “Priestley uses the metaphor of…” For wider-text work, range across the whole play. Cover at least two or three different moments from different acts. Use topic sentences: “Elsewhere, Priestley presents this theme when…” Always embed AO4 (context) into your analysis rather than adding it as a separate paragraph.

Pulling It Together: How Themes Connect

In the exam, the strongest answers show how themes interconnect. Responsibility connects to class (the Birlings avoid responsibility because they see the working class as beneath concern). Class connects to gender (Eva’s exploitation is worse because she is both working class and female). The generational divide connects to morality (the young develop conscience; the old do not). Priestley designed these themes to reinforce each other, so an answer that links them demonstrates the deepest understanding of the play.
before.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • The five key themes — responsibility, class, generational divide, gender, and morality — are interconnected. The strongest exam answers show how they reinforce each other.
  • Priestley’s central argument is that personal and collective responsibility are inseparable: individuals must accept their guilt, and society must build systems that protect the vulnerable.
  • For the Eduqas two-part question, part (a) requires close analysis of the extract (AO2 focus), while part (b) requires range across the play with embedded context (AO4). Both parts reward analysis of Priestley’s methods, not just description of events.
before.exam_tip_html: For the Eduqas 40-mark question, spend roughly 20 minutes on each part. In part (a), aim for 3 detailed analytical points from the extract with embedded quotations. In part (b), aim for 3 points from different parts of the play. Every paragraph should contain: a point about Priestley’s purpose, a quotation, analysis of language/structure (AO2), and a link to context (AO4). The examiner is looking for ‘how Priestley presents’ — always foreground the writer’s choices.

flashcard_questions.q: How does Eva's five-stage journey argue for systemic change?

practice_questions.text: Read an extract from the Inspector’s final speech. How does Priestley present the theme of responsibility in this extract? [20]
practice_questions.marks:
Top band (17–20) Sophisticated analysis. ‘We are members of one body’ — biblical allusion gives collective responsibility religious authority. ‘Millions and millions’ — repetition emphasises the scale of injustice. ‘Responsible for each other’ — direct, declarative statement of Priestley’s thesis. AO2 + AO4 throughout.

Upper-mid band (13–16) Detailed analysis.

Mid band (9–12) Some relevant points.

Lower-mid band (5–8) Basic.

Lower band (1–4) Minimal.

practice_questions.text: How does Priestley present the theme of class across the whole play? [20]
practice_questions.marks:
Top band (17–20) Convincing analysis. Birling: ‘cheap labour.’ Mrs Birling: ‘girls of that class.’ Gerald’s power over Daisy. Sheila’s ability to sack Eva. The class system enables exploitation at every level. Priestley’s purpose: to dismantle class prejudice.

Upper-mid band (13–16) Clear analysis across the play.

Mid band (9–12) Some relevant points.

Lower-mid band (5–8) Limited.

Lower band (1–4) Simple.

practice_questions.text: Read the section where Mrs Birling describes Eva as one of ‘girls of that class.’ How does Priestley present class prejudice in this extract? [20]
practice_questions.marks:
Top band (17–20) Perceptive analysis. ‘That class’ — the demonstrative determiner creates psychological distance. ‘Gross’ — adjective dehumanises Eva. Formal, controlled language mirrors institutional coldness. Priestley: the charity system is another mechanism of class power.

Upper-mid band (13–16) Detailed analysis.

Mid band (9–12) Some awareness.

Lower-mid band (5–8) Basic.

Lower band (1–4) Minimal.

practice_questions.text: How does Priestley present the theme of gender and exploitation elsewhere in the play? [20]
practice_questions.marks:
Top band (17–20) Convincing analysis. Eva’s journey maps women’s limited options. Gerald’s affair: power imbalance. Eric’s assault: male violence. Mrs Birling’s rejection: even women enforce patriarchal class structures. Double standards: men are forgiven, women are destroyed.

Upper-mid band (13–16) Clear analysis.

Mid band (9–12) Some relevant points.

Lower-mid band (5–8) Limited.

Lower band (1–4) Simple.

practice_questions.text: “The play’s message about responsibility is as relevant today as it was in 1945.” How far do you agree? [20]
practice_questions.marks:
Top band (17–20) Sophisticated argument. Priestley’s themes of class, exploitation, and collective responsibility remain relevant. Modern parallels: inequality, corporate responsibility, welfare debate. The cyclical structure suggests the lesson is never fully learned. Counter: specific 1912/1945 context is historically specific.

Upper-mid band (13–16) Clear argument.

Mid band (9–12) Some relevant points.

Lower-mid band (5–8) Basic.

Lower band (1–4) Minimal.

practice_questions.text: Explore how Priestley uses the character of Sheila to convey his message about moral conscience. Refer to her development across the play. [20]
practice_questions.marks:
Top band (17–20) Perceptive tracking. Act 1: spoilt, materialistic (‘Oh — it’s wonderful!’). After confession: genuine shame. Act 2: returns ring, warns Gerald. Act 3: ‘You’re pretending everything’s just as it was before.’ Sheila models Priestley’s ideal audience response: recognise guilt, feel remorse, change behaviour.

Upper-mid band (13–16) Clear tracking.

Mid band (9–12) Some awareness.

Lower-mid band (5–8) Basic.

Lower band (1–4) Simple.
